chapter_summary:
While ad-hoc commands are useful for quick, one-off tasks, the true power of Ansible lies in **playbooks**. Playbooks are YAML-formatted files that define a set of ordered tasks to be executed on specified hosts. They are the core of Ansible automation, allowing you to orchestrate complex multi-step workflows, configure systems to a desired state, and deploy applications in a repeatable and version-controlled manner. Think of a playbook as a recipe for your infrastructure: it describes exactly what ingredients (tasks) to use and in what order, to achieve a specific culinary outcome (system state). Because playbooks are text files, they can be stored in version control systems like Git, enabling collaboration, change tracking, and easy rollback.

A typical Ansible playbook starts with `---` (YAML document start marker) and is a list of one or more "plays." Each play targets a specific group of hosts and defines a series of tasks to run on those hosts. The basic structure of a play includes:
*   `name`: A human-readable description of the play.
*   `hosts`: Specifies which hosts or groups from your inventory this play will run against.
*   `become`: (Optional) Set to `yes` or `true` if tasks in this play require elevated privileges (e.g., `sudo`).
*   `vars`: (Optional) Defines variables specific to this play.
*   `tasks`: A list of individual tasks to be executed.

Each task within a play also has a `name` and then calls an **Ansible module**. Modules are reusable units of code that Ansible executes on the managed nodes. Ansible comes with a vast collection of modules, covering almost every system administration need: package management (`ansible.builtin.dnf`, `ansible.builtin.apt`), service management (`ansible.builtin.service`), file manipulation (`ansible.builtin.copy`, `ansible.builtin.file`), user and group management (`ansible.builtin.user`, `ansible.builtin.group`), and much more. When you invoke a module, you pass it arguments (parameters) to specify its behavior.

Let's look at a simple playbook example to install the Nginx web server and ensure its service is running and enabled:

```yaml
---
- name: Configure Nginx web server
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes # This play requires root privileges
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nginx
        state: present

    - name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: yes

    - name: Ensure Nginx configuration file is present
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        src: files/nginx.conf
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: '0644'
      notify: restart nginx # This handler will be triggered if the file changes

  handlers: # Handlers are tasks that only run when notified
    - name: restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
```

To execute this playbook, you would use the `ansible-playbook` command: `ansible-playbook -i ~/my_inventory.ini nginx_config.yml`.
In this example, the `ansible.builtin.dnf` module ensures the `nginx` package is `present`. If Nginx is already installed, Ansible will detect this and report "ok" without making any changes, demonstrating **idempotency**. If it's not installed, it will install it. Similarly, the `ansible.builtin.service` module ensures the `nginx` service is `started` and `enabled` to start on boot. The `ansible.builtin.copy` module copies a local `nginx.conf` file from the control node's `files` directory to `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` on the managed node. Notice the `notify: restart nginx` directive. This is a powerful feature: the `restart nginx` handler (defined in the `handlers` section) will *only* be triggered if the `copy` task actually makes a change (i.e., the `nginx.conf` file on the managed node was different from the source). This prevents unnecessary service restarts, further enhancing efficiency and idempotency.

Common mistakes when writing playbooks often revolve around YAML syntax. YAML is very sensitive to indentation; use spaces, not tabs, and be consistent. A common error is misaligning a task or module parameter, which will cause the `ansible-playbook` command to fail with a parsing error. Always double-check your indentation. Another frequent issue is incorrect module parameters or forgetting required parameters. Refer to the official Ansible documentation for each module (`ansible-doc <module_name>`) to ensure you're using the correct arguments and values. For instance, `state: present` is common, but `state: absent` would remove a package or file, and `state: latest` would ensure the newest version of a package. Understanding these nuances is key to writing effective playbooks. Safety note: Always test your playbooks in a development or staging environment before deploying them to production, especially those that make significant system changes or restart critical services.

screens.title: Understanding Ansible Playbooks and Modules
screens.subtitle: Authoring repeatable automation: plays, tasks, modules, handlers, and idempotency

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn what makes an Ansible playbook the foundation of reliable automation. A playbook is a structured text file written in YAML that defines ordered plays and tasks, and it serves as a recipe to reach a defined system state. You will see how plays target groups of hosts, how tasks invoke modules like the package or service modules, and how handlers and notifications help avoid unnecessary restarts. Understanding idempotency is central: modules report if they changed state or if the target was already correct, which allows safe repeated runs. We'll also cover common YAML pitfalls and a hands-on example that installs and configures a web server, so you can run, inspect results, and interpret OK versus CHANGED statuses. By the end you should be able to read a playbook, spot a task, and reason about whether a task will change a system before you run it. As a concrete example, you'll follow a playbook that installs Nginx, ensures it is started and enabled, copies a configuration file, and triggers a restart handler only when the file actually changes. Notice that treating playbooks as versioned recipes supports collaboration and safe rollbacks. Think about the next playbook you will write: what state must your systems reach, and how will a module express that state?

keyIdea.title: Playbooks are repeatable recipes
keyIdea.text: Playbooks declare desired system state with ordered tasks and modules so automation is predictable, idempotent, and versionable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus your practice and give clear milestones for competency. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and structure of an Ansible playbook: why plays exist, how hosts and become control scope, and how tasks are arranged. Second, you'll identify and use common Ansible modules such as the package manager module, the service module, and the copy module to perform routine administration. Third, you'll write a basic playbook that installs packages and manages services, applying variables and handlers where needed. Fourth, you will understand idempotency and be able to debug YAML parsing and parameter errors that prevent a playbook from running. Each objective includes a short rationale and a mnemonic to help retention. Treat these as checkpoints: explain the structure aloud, create a simple playbook, run it in a lab, and read the playbook output to verify OK versus CHANGED. That practice will convert knowledge into a verified competency you can use on a control node safely.

keyIdea.title: Four practical milestones
keyIdea.text: Explain playbooks, use modules, author a basic playbook, and debug YAML and module errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Continued)
screens.subtitle: How these skills connect to safe automation practice

narration.text: These complementary objectives connect the skills so your automation is safe and maintainable. When you can identify modules and their parameters, you reduce runtime errors. Writing a playbook in a version-controlled directory lets you review changes, roll back, and collaborate. Understanding idempotency means you can schedule repeated runs without fear of repeated side-effects. Debugging YAML errors is often the first practical skill you use; consistent spacing and clear parameter alignment prevent parsing failures. As an example, misaligned module parameters commonly produce a parsing error before Ansible executes any remote tasks. Practically, you will create a playbook that installs a web server, opens firewall ports, and places a simple index file. Then you will run it in a staging environment and use the playbook output to confirm whether tasks made changes. This workflow — author, test, inspect, iterate — is what keeps automation healthy. A useful mnemonic is R-I-D-E: Read structure, Identify modules, Draft playbook, Execute and verify. That process reduces surprises when you move to production.

keyIdea.title: From authoring to safe execution
keyIdea.text: Combine module knowledge, idempotency, and debugging practice to build reliable playbooks you can run in staging before production.

screens.title: What is a Playbook?
screens.subtitle: Playbooks as ordered YAML recipes for desired system state

narration.text: A playbook is a YAML-formatted file that defines one or more plays, and each play contains the set of tasks that will be executed on targeted hosts. Think of it as a recipe: each play declares which hosts to operate on, whether to run with elevated privileges, and the exact steps needed to reach the desired state. This structure matters because it enables reproducible automation: the same playbook applied twice should either leave the system unchanged or report that required changes were made. A concrete example is a playbook that installs a web server package, ensures the service is started, and copies a configuration file. The playbook begins with a YAML document marker and lists plays with keys such as name, hosts, become, vars, and tasks. A common misconception is to think playbooks execute tasks in parallel across plays; while tasks within a play run in order on each host, multiple plays allow you to target different groups in sequence. Another pitfall is treating ad-hoc commands like a replacement for proper playbooks — ad-hoc commands are fine for quick checks, but playbooks are better for repeatable changes and version control. To check your understanding: can you describe which key would tell Ansible to use sudo on managed nodes and why that might be necessary for package or service management?

keyIdea.title: Playbook = ordered recipe
keyIdea.text: A playbook sequences plays and tasks in YAML so you can express and reproduce desired system states.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a Playbook?

Playbooks as YAML recipes

Playbooks declare plays, targets, privilege escalation, variables, and an ordered list of tasks that invoke modules to reach a desired state.

Definition

A playbook is a YAML file composed of plays. Each play targets hosts and includes tasks, optional vars, and handlers. The playbook format makes automation readable and versionable.

Common play keys
  • name: human-readable label for the play
  • hosts: inventory group or hosts to run against
  • become: set to yes when privilege escalation is needed
  • tasks: ordered list of task entries that call modules
Analogy
Like a cookbook recipe: the playbook lists ingredients, steps, and whether a special tool or privilege is needed to complete the step.
Concrete example (conceptual)
---
- name: Configure Nginx web server
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nginx
        state: present

    - name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: yes
This snippet shows a simple play that installs and starts a package and service. Use it as a starting point for more tasks and handlers.
Key Takeaway

Playbooks make automation declarative and repeatable; they should be versioned and tested in staging.

screens.title: Plays, Hosts, and Privilege Escalation
screens.subtitle: How plays target inventory and when to use become

narration.text: Plays are the organizational unit inside a playbook that declare which hosts should receive a set of tasks. The hosts key references your inventory groups or explicit hostnames and scopes the play's actions. Using become set to yes tells Ansible to run tasks with elevated privileges on the managed nodes, which is often required for package installation, service control, and modifying system files. As a concrete example, a play targeting the webservers group will execute its tasks sequentially on each host in that group, and if the tasks require root privileges, you include become: yes either at the play level or per task. A subtle misconception is thinking become always runs commands as root on the control node; it only affects execution on the managed nodes during the play. Another important point is variable scoping: vars declared at the play level apply to tasks in that play, whereas inventory or host vars can override play vars. In practice, structure plays so that hosts with similar needs are grouped together and privileged operations are minimized. A quick verification step is to run your playbook in a staging environment and watch whether tasks that require become fail due to missing sudo rights, which signals you need to adjust privilege settings in inventory or your user configuration. What host group would you create for database servers if they need a different set of privileged operations?

keyIdea.title: Plays scope tasks to hosts
keyIdea.text: Use hosts to target inventory groups and become to escalate privileges on managed nodes when required by modules.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Plays, Hosts, and Become

Scoping actions with plays

Organize plays by host groups and privilege needs to reduce risk and keep variables scoped correctly.

How plays execute
  1. Resolve hosts from inventory into a list of managed nodes.
  2. Apply play-level vars and determine privilege escalation if become is set.
  3. Run tasks in order on each host, reporting OK/CHANGED/FAILED per host.
Misconception
become affects managed nodes only; it doesn't change how the control node operates. Use become selectively to reduce security exposure.
Example scenario
You have a webservers group and a dbservers group. Place package installs and service management for webservers in a play that targets webservers with become enabled. Keep database maintenance tasks in a separate play targeting dbservers so you can apply different variables or handlers.
Key Takeaway

Structure playbooks by host role and privilege to keep changes minimal and auditable.

screens.title: Modules: Common Tasks and When to Use Them
screens.subtitle: dnf, service, copy, user, and firewalld modules explained

narration.text: Ansible modules are the units of work that tasks invoke on managed nodes. Each module performs a specific function, and choosing the correct module and parameters determines whether your playbook is idempotent and predictable. For package management on Red Hat systems use the dnf module; it accepts parameters like name and state where state can be present, absent, or latest. The service module manages services and their enabled or running state. The copy module moves files from the control node to managed nodes, with ownership and mode options, and it can notify handlers if the file changed. The user module ensures user accounts are present or absent and can set shell and home directory. The firewalld module from the ansible. posix collection manages firewall services and can be used to enable services like http permanently. A common misconception is to use shell commands when a module exists; shell tasks are more error-prone and less idempotent. A concrete example: using the dnf module to ensure nginx is present and the service module to set it started and enabled produces deterministic output and safe repeats. When deciding which module to use, always prefer the dedicated module over running package manager commands directly, because modules understand state and return structured results. Which module would you pick to add a system user with a specific shell and home directory?

keyIdea.title: Pick purpose-built modules
keyIdea.text: Prefer ansible modules over shell commands so tasks are idempotent and report clear outcomes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Common Modules

Modules for system administration

Modules encapsulate common tasks so playbooks remain idempotent and clear.

ansible.builtin.dnf
Manages packages on RHEL/CentOS/Fedora family. Common parameter: name, state (present, absent, latest).
ansible.builtin.service
Controls services. Common parameters: name, state (started, stopped, restarted), enabled (yes/no).
ansible.builtin.copy
Copies a file from control node to managed node and can set owner, group, and mode. It supports notify to trigger handlers on change.
ansible.builtin.user
Manages user accounts, shell, home directory, and state (present/absent).
ansible.posix.firewalld
Manages firewalld zones and services; can enable a service permanently and reload rules via handlers.
Why not shell?
Shell or command tasks are less idempotent and harder to interpret; prefer built-in modules that describe desired state.
Example
Use the dnf module to ensure nginx is present, then the service module to ensure it is started and enabled. The copy task can notify a restart handler only when the configuration file changed.

screens.title: Handlers and notify: Efficient Service Restarts
screens.subtitle: Trigger actions only when a change occurs

narration.text: Handlers are special tasks defined in a playbook that run only when notified by another task. This pattern prevents unnecessary service restarts and improves efficiency and safety. When a copy task updates a configuration file, it can include a notify directive that names a handler, for example restart nginx. If the copy task detected a change on the managed node, Ansible registers that notification and executes the handler at the end of the play or at a designated point. A common mistake is defining a handler but never notifying it, causing changes to be applied without triggering the necessary restart, or conversely notifying a handler when no change occurred which would be inefficient. For a concrete example, copy a new nginx. conf to /etc/nginx/nginx. conf and notify restart nginx; the handler contains a service module call to restart the nginx service. This ensures the service restarts only when the configuration file changed, not every run. Consider the order of operations: handlers execute after all tasks in a play by default, making them suitable for finalizing state. A verification step is to run the playbook twice; the first run may show CHANGED with the handler running, and the second run should show OK for the copy task and the handler should not run. Why is that behavior important for production systems?

keyIdea.title: Handlers run on notification
keyIdea.text: Use notify and handlers to avoid unnecessary service restarts and to ensure changes are applied only when needed.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Handlers & Notify

Only restart services when needed

Handlers run when tasks notify them, ensuring actions like service restarts happen only after real changes.

Process
Task runs and reports whether it changed a resource. If changed and it includes a notify directive, a handler is queued.
Handlers run after the task list completes for that play. They are idempotent tasks in their own right; a handler should use a module like service with the desired state.
Concrete example
- name: Ensure Nginx configuration file is present
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    src: files/nginx.conf
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  notify: restart nginx

handlers:
  - name: restart nginx
    ansible.builtin.service:
      name: nginx
      state: restarted
The copy task only triggers the handler when it makes a change. Run the playbook twice to observe the handler running only once.
Key Takeaway

Handlers minimize disruption by running only when notified; use them for restarts, reloads, and finalization steps.

screens.title: Idempotency: Predictable, Repeatable Runs
screens.subtitle: Why Ansible reports OK or CHANGED and how that supports safe automation

narration.text: Idempotency is the property that applying the same playbook multiple times leaves the system in the same state after the first change. In practical terms, modules implement idempotency by checking current state and only making changes when necessary. When a task finds the desired state is already present, Ansible reports OK for that host; when it had to make a change, it reports CHANGED. For example, if a task ensures a package is present and the package already exists, the dnf module will return OK. If the package is missing, it will install it and return CHANGED. Understanding this distinction is essential for interpreting playbook output and designing safe automation. A common misunderstanding is to treat CHANGED as an error — instead, CHANGED indicates that Ansible made a planned change. Also, avoid writing tasks with idempotency baked into shell commands; modules provide structured comparisons and return values. A quick check is to run a playbook twice: the first run may show CHANGED for tasks that modified state, and the second run should show OK for unchanged items. Reflect: when you schedule automation to run regularly, idempotency ensures it enforces the desired state without creating additional side effects. How would you validate that a handler ran only when a configuration file changed?

keyIdea.title: Idempotency drives safety
keyIdea.text: Idempotent modules detect existing state and only make changes when needed, producing OK or CHANGED results that guide verification.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Idempotency

Idempotency keeps runs safe

Idempotent modules check current state and change only when necessary. Use this to schedule safe, repeatable runs.

Definition

Idempotency means reapplying the same playbook results in no further changes once the desired state is reached. Modules implement checks and report OK or CHANGED.

Misconception

CHANGED is not an error. It indicates the module made a planned, expected change to reach desired state.

Practical verification
  1. Run the playbook once and observe CHANGED results for modified resources.
  2. Run the playbook a second time; idempotent tasks should report OK if no changes were needed.
  3. Check handlers only ran when notified after a CHANGED event.
Pro tip

Prefer modules that express desired state rather than shell commands; they return structured results that help you reason about idempotency.

screens.title: Hands-on Playbook: webserver_setup.yml
screens.subtitle: Live-code style review of a webserver setup playbook

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete playbook you can author and run: a webserver setup that installs httpd, ensures the service is running, opens the HTTP firewall port, and places a simple index page. Start by creating a playbook file in your projects folder and include a play targeting a servers group with become set to yes so package and service operations succeed. The tasks call the dnf package module to install httpd, the service module to start and enable httpd, the firewalld module to open HTTP service permanently (noting that this requires the ansible. posix collection), and the copy module to write a simple index. html. Handlers include a reload for firewalld so changes to firewall rules apply only when necessary. A common mistake is forgetting to install a collection when using a module from it; if a module is not found, install the collection or use an alternative. Another frequent error is YAML indentation: use consistent spaces and avoid tabs. As a verification step, run the ansible-playbook command pointing to your inventory and observe the output. After running, SSH into a managed node and confirm the httpd service status and that the index page is reachable. How would you modify this playbook to deploy Nginx instead of Apache?

keyIdea.title: Practical playbook example
keyIdea.text: A webserver playbook demonstrates modules, handlers, firewall rules, and a simple content deploy to validate end-to-end automation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › webserver_setup.yml Walkthrough

Live-code style playbook

A ready-to-run playbook that installs Apache, opens the firewall, and writes an index page, with a handler to reload the firewall when needed.

Starter playbook
---
- name: Configure basic web server with Apache
  hosts: servers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure httpd package is installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: httpd
        state: present

    - name: Ensure httpd service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: httpd
        state: started
        enabled: yes

    - name: Open firewall port for HTTP (80/tcp)
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        service: http
        permanent: yes
        state: enabled
      notify: reload firewalld

    - name: Create a simple index.html file
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        content: "<h1>Hello from Ansible!</h1>"
        dest: /var/www/html/index.html
        owner: apache
        group: apache
        mode: '0644'

  handlers:
    - name: reload firewalld
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: firewalld
        state: reloaded
Save this file as webserver_setup.yml under your ansible_projects directory and run it with the ansible-playbook command against your inventory to observe results.
Notes & checks
  • Install ansible.posix collection if the firewalld module is missing.
  • Use become for package and service tasks so they run with elevated rights on managed nodes.
  • Run the playbook twice: first run may show CHANGED, second run should show OK for idempotent tasks.
Common mistake

Using tabs or inconsistent spaces leads to YAML parsing errors before Ansible runs any tasks.

screens.title: YAML Syntax and Debugging Playbook Errors
screens.subtitle: Common parsing errors, module parameter mistakes, and how to fix them

narration.text: YAML syntax errors are among the most common reasons a playbook fails to run. YAML is indentation-sensitive; use spaces not tabs, and maintain consistent indentation levels for plays, tasks, and module parameters. Typical errors include misaligned module parameters that cause a parsing error, or using a module parameter name that the module does not accept. To debug, first read the ansible-playbook parser error: it will point to a line number where it failed to interpret YAML structure. If the error references an unexpected key, verify that the module parameters are indented under the module name and not at the task level. Another helpful technique is to run ansible-lint or a YAML validator to catch problems before execution. For module parameter mistakes, consult the module's documentation via ansible-doc to confirm valid parameters and their types. A practical debugging example: if a copy task uses mode: 0644 without quotes, YAML can interpret it as an octal number; best practice is to quote file modes as a string. Also ensure required collections are installed when modules live outside the core collection. A final verification step is to run the playbook against a small test host with increased verbosity to inspect which task failed and why. When you find a parsing or parameter error, correct indentation or parameter names and rerun; this iterative approach quickly surfaces and resolves YAML issues. What command would you run to view module documentation locally?

keyIdea.title: Read errors, fix indentation
keyIdea.text: YAML parsing errors usually point to indentation or misplaced keys; use validators and ansible-doc to confirm module parameters.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › YAML Syntax & Debugging

Avoid parsing and parameter errors

Use consistent spaces, validate YAML, and check module docs to resolve errors quickly.

Quick checklist
  • Use spaces not tabs and keep indentation consistent.
  • Ensure module parameters are nested under the module name.
  • Quote file modes and other ambiguous values as strings.
  • Install required collections for non-core modules.
Debugging steps
  1. Read the parser error and note the indicated line number.
  2. Open the playbook and check indentation around that line.
  3. Confirm module parameter names using module documentation.
  4. Run with increased verbosity to see where execution stops.
Example fix

If a copy task shows a parser error because mode is unquoted, change mode: 0644 to mode: '0644' to avoid numeric interpretation issues.

screens.title: Run the Playbook and Interpret Output
screens.subtitle: Understanding OK, CHANGED, and failed states and verifying results

narration.text: Running a playbook produces structured output that tells you which tasks ran, whether they changed state, and if any failures occurred. After you execute a playbook against your inventory, review the summary: tasks marked OK indicate the desired state was already present, CHANGED means the module altered the system to reach desired state, and FAILED indicates an error that prevented completion. A practical workflow is to run the playbook in a staging inventory, observe the first-run CHANGED results, and then re-run the playbook to confirm idempotency with OK results. For example, when you install httpd the first run may show CHANGED for the package task and start the service, while the second run should show OK for both package and service tasks if nothing else changed. If a task fails, examine the error to see if it is a YAML parsing error, a missing module or collection, or a permission problem; adjust the playbook or inventory accordingly and re-run. As a verification step, log into a managed node and confirm the service status and firewall rules, and curl the index page to validate the deployed content. A useful question to guide your checks is: did any handler run, and if so, was it triggered by a CHANGED task that you expected to alter system behavior?

keyIdea.title: Read output, verify state
keyIdea.text: Interpret OK and CHANGED to confirm idempotency, inspect failures for parsing or permission issues, and verify systems directly after runs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Execute & Interpret

Run, then verify

Use staging runs to observe CHANGED versus OK, handle failures, and validate system state directly on managed nodes.

Reading results
  • OK: desired state already present, no changes.
  • CHANGED: module made changes to reach desired state.
  • FAILED: error prevented task completion; examine the message and fix the playbook or environment.
Verification steps
  1. Run the playbook in staging and observe the output summary.
  2. SSH into a managed node and check service status and firewall settings.
  3. Use a simple HTTP request from the control node to confirm the index page is served.
Common failure causes
  • YAML parsing errors due to bad indentation.
  • Missing collections or incorrect module names.
  • Insufficient privileges on the managed node when become is not set.
Check your thinking

If a handler ran, determine which task notified it and whether that notification matched your expectation for a real change.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep three ideas at the center of your practice: playbooks are YAML recipes that express desired state; modules are the purpose-built actions you use inside tasks; and idempotency plus handlers let you run automation safely and efficiently. A playbook's organization into plays, hosts, become, tasks, and handlers makes it readable and versionable. Choose modules like the dnf, service, copy, user, and firewalld modules for common administration needs rather than shell commands, and prefer module parameters that express desired state. When debugging, read parser errors for line numbers, fix indentation errors, and consult module documentation for valid parameters. Finally, always test in staging and verify the system state directly after a run. These habits turn playbooks into reliable infrastructure code you can trust to reduce configuration drift and improve operational consistency.

What to Remember

Playbook
A YAML file that sequences plays, tasks, and handlers to express desired system state.
Modules
Use built-in modules like dnf, service, copy and user to perform repeatable administration tasks.
Idempotency & Handlers
Handlers run only when notified by changed tasks, keeping runs efficient and predictable.
Final takeaway

Author playbooks as reviewed, idempotent recipes, prefer modules over shell, test in staging, and read outputs to confirm behavior.

Together these practices reduce accidental outages and make automation safe to run repeatedly. Use staging runs and direct verification to confirm outcomes before any production rollout. Playbook Structure

Author concise playbooks, choose the right modules, and test runs to ensure safe, repeatable automation across your systems.
